content:
Students currently enrolled in an Advanced Placementcourse at The
Frederick Gunn School are required to sit for AdvancedPlacement
Exams. Only students taking an Advanced Placementcourse at The
Frederick Gunn School will sit for an Advanced PlacementExam. The
Frederick Gunn School will not offer Advanced PlacementExams for
courses not supported at The Frederick Gunn Schoolduring the
current year.

For the start of the 2021-2022 school year, formaldaytime study halls
will not be assigned as they have in the past. Studentswill work with
their advisor to identify blocks of time in the weekto set aside as study
time. In some cases, additional mandatory study halltimes will be
determined in conjunction with the Academic Office.

Evening study hall (ESH) begins at 8:00 p.m. and endsat 10:00 p.m.
Sunday through Thursday. On Fridays in the fall, allboarding freshmen
will attend an evening study skills session beginningat 8:00 p.m. Day
students are encouraged to participate if interested.On Fridays, study
hall will begin at 8:30 p.m.During designated studyhall hours, students
in the dorms are expected to be in their rooms completingschool
work, independently. Students are not permitted toshower during
study hall hours. Evening Study Hall should be libraryquiet and
students should be focused on school work. Streamingservices such
as Netflix, Hulu, etc., video games or the use ofmusical instruments are
not permitted during Evening Study Hall. Juniors andseniors will be
permitted to use the library and TPACC as additionalstudy spaces
during study hall. Freshmen and Sophomores will haveaccess to
TPACC for portions of study hall during the year.Students enrolled in a
music course will be permitted to use music practicerooms for
instrument practice in the evenings. All spaces oncampus must
The Frederick Gunn School Student Handbook13
maintain study conditions during study hall hours, though students
are permitted to do group work in TPACC and the Library.
WhenQuiet Hoursare held instead of Evening StudyHall all
students will maintain a respectful dormitory environment,as directed
by dorm parents.
Note to parents and friends:For the purpose of ensuringquiet study
conditions, we request telephoning, texting, or emailingduring times
when study conditions are not in effect. We also requestthat parents
do not request taking their children off campus (i.e.to dinner) during
Evening Study Hall hours.

The Tisch Family Library contains millions of digitaland print resources
for academic and recreational use. The Library isopen for study and
research during the following hours: Monday - Friday7:45 a.m.10:00
p.m.; Saturday 7:45 a.m.Noon; and Sunday 7:00 p.m.10:00p.m. The
Library is closed Saturday afternoon and evening.
The Library is a shared academic space for the entireFrederick Gunn
School community. Please observe these guidelinesin the library: 1)
Act respectfully and responsibly to avoid disturbingthose working and
studying nearby. 2) Moderate your volume when talkingand mute all
your devices. Take voice/video calls outside the library.3) Remember
to observe all school rules.

At The Frederick Gunn School, every student is matchedwith a faculty
advisor. Advisors meet formally twice weekly withtheir advisees and
maintain frequent contact both formally and informally.The advisor
guides students toward understanding their academicresponsibilities,
formulating realistic goals, making course selectionsto build a
challenging transcript, and often assists in managingpersonal and
behavioral issues. Personal conferences among parents,advisors, and
teachers are an important function of the fall ParentsWeekend and
these conferences establish relationships that willbe sustained
throughout a students tenure at The Frederick GunnSchool.
The Frederick Gunn School Student Handbook14
With the exception of new students who are assigned advisors,
returning students may select advisors. In order to change advisors
there is a formal petition process. Students shouldconnect with the
Dean of Students office to discuss and initiate thisprocess.

To protect the relationship between faculty/advisorsand students
from conflict and to preserve its usefulness to students,The Frederick
Gunn School has established the following policy ofconfidentiality:
Private discussions between a student and a memberof the faculty
from whom the student seeks counsel or advice shallnormally be
considered confidential. It is assumed that a studentseeking greater
self-understanding or facing a difficult decisionmay wish to talk out
feelings and concerns, and may, in the process ofdoing so, discuss
behavior as well as values. However, students shouldbe aware that
disclosure of rule violations or other matters mayneed to be reported
to the Dean of Students or to legal authorities. Specifically,any
information that meets the standard of mandated reportingmust be
shared with the Dean of Students, who then must shareit with legal
authorities or the Department of Children and Families.It is, therefore,
an inherent part of the confidential counseling relationshipthat the
faculty member has the right to seek professionaladvice and counsel
of the Dean of Students, Director of Counseling, HealthCenter, or the
Head of School with regard to a particular counselingrelationship. If
information is shared, it is still held in the strictestof confidence and
will not be shared except as necessary for the well-beingof the
student, other community members, or the school.
The policy of confidentiality should not be construedas an implication
that rule violations are condoned if they are revealedin a counseling
environment. The policy does indicate that the schoolbelieves that, in
an individual case of voluntary disclosure, the personalgrowth and
development of the student may be more important thanthe belated
enforcement of a particular rule. However, that doesnot mean that
students who disclose rule violations to an advisorwill not be subject
to discipline. If a student has any questions regardingthe nature of
confidentiality and its use in a counseling situation,the student should
The Frederick Gunn School Student Handbook15
seek the advice of their advisor, the Director of Counseling, Health
Center, or the Dean of Students.

The Frederick Gunn Schools discipline philosophyrests on the premise
that students can learn and grow from their mistakesthrough a
supported process of self-reflection. Moral development,within the
discipline system, occurs through thoughtful and intentional
conversations between faculty members and students,combined
with consequences. These conversations and consequencesseek to
aid students in understanding their role and responsibilitywithin a
larger community. The Frederick Gunn School valuesthese
conversations and believes parental involvement tobe crucial in a
students ability to fully learn from the experience.We find that this
process of dialogue is more effective in guiding ourstudents
decisions than the fear of punitive discipline. Ourfaculty members
draw guidance from the schools core values of respect,responsibility,
integrity, and scholarship to ensure that each uniquedisciplinary
situation is handled consistently and objectively.Our discipline
philosophy guides the conversations we have, the policieswe create,
and the decisions we make. With this approach we areable to provide
each student with the greatest opportunity for moralgrowth and
development.
The Frederick Gunn School has a deep respect for thewelfare of each
individual; relationships are characterized by trust,honesty,
cooperation, civility, and respect for property. Webelieve a student
can benefit significantly from working through a disciplinarysystem
that encourages reflection and restoration withinthe community. It is
usually only after a second major offense at the Probationarylevel (or
a succession of offenses that cumulatively equal asecond Probation),
that a student may be separated from the school.
Students should note that a disciplinary status mightbe attained in
either of two ways: Through a single serious mistakein judgment or by
the accumulation of missed Commitment Absence (CA)(see
Attendance section) or Disciplinary Points (DP) asoutlined below.
The Frederick Gunn School Student Handbook16
Behavior posted on social media that comes to the attention of
faculty or the Dean of Students may also have a disciplinaryresponse
from The Frederick Gunn School.
Students bear the responsibility for removal of anassigned
Commitment Absence or Disciplinary Point due to a
misunderstanding.The Commitment Absence or DisciplinaryPoint
must be removed within one week of the offense.Studentsare not
permitted to work off any CAs or DPs. The Dean ofStudents office
completes weekly Commitment Absence and DisciplinePoint audits
at the end of the academic week.
Rule violations are classified under three headings:Status Warning
(SW), Discipline Warning (DW), and Probation (PRO).
Students must be aware that discipline carries overfrom the end of
one year to the beginning of the next year.
Prefects placed on lower levels of discipline willbe temporarily
removed from their position during their disciplinaryperiod.
Prefects placed on Probation will be permanently removedfrom
their position for the remainder of the year. Studentswho go on
Probation at or after the beginning of junior yearare ineligible to run
for Prefect, as are students who are on DisciplineWarning or
Probation during the Prefect election process.

The following violations fall under the DisciplinaryPoint system:
2  Late to commitment (11-20 mins)
2  Campus Contribution absence
1  Late to commitment (0-10 mins)
1  Failure to sign-in or sign-out (SISO)
1 - Dress code
1 - Community Disrespect, which includes but is notlimited to:
Offensive language
Dorm issues - failure to clean or complete dorm jobs,late to
check-in, failure to carry key/FOB, failure to followdorm rules,
etc.
Formal meal absences
The Frederick Gunn School Student Handbook17
General disrespect whether inside or outside our community
Accumulation of Discipline Points
12, 18, or 24 points (of various point violations):
Students are placed on Status Warning (12 points),Discipline
Warning (18 points), or Probation (24 points). Seediscipline
levels below.
8 or 16 points (of the same point violation):
Students are placed on Discipline Warning (8 points),or
Probation (16 points). See discipline levels below.
32 points (of various point violations) or 24 (ofthe same violation)
Students will have a meeting with the Dean of Studentsand
Head of School to determine their future at The FrederickGunn
School. The schools response may include an immediate
Discipline Committee hearing or immediate dismissal.

Students placed on Status Warning will be requiredto meet with the
Dean of Students office, their advisor, and parent(as available),
check-in Monday through Friday between 7:30 a.m. and8:00 a.m. in
the Hallway of Flags for two weeks and complete 3hours of on

If a student has demonstrated during the Probationaryperiod a
significant, positive effort and improved contributionto every facet of
school life through the completion of their educationalModule and
community hours, the student will be considered forremoval from
Probation. The student will meet with the Dean ofStudents to discuss
their learning and growth and make a plan for avoidingfuture serious
discipline.
The Dean, sometimes in consultation with the Headof School or the
faculty, will then decide to remove the student fromProbation based
The Frederick Gunn School Student Handbook22
on: the students engagement with the Probation process, the
students recent disciplinary record, attendance record(classes,
sports, meals, etc.), and general campus behavior.Students who
have not engaged seriously in this process or do notmeet with the
Dean of Students at the end of their probationaryperiods will stay on
Probation until additional conditions are met or themeeting with the
Dean of Students occurs.
Students who are removed from Probation remain ina remedial
period for one year following the date of their removalfrom Probation.
If students commit an additional Probationary offenseduring that
time, they will go to a Discipline Committee Hearingand will likely be
required to withdraw from The Frederick Gunn School.

Students who commit another disciplinary offense whilealready on
discipline must finish their first disciplinary offenseresponsibilities
before they can begin serving their next disciplineoffense.
Students on SW and who commit another SW offense willbe
placed on DW.
Students who commit three (3) separate SW offensesin the
course of the year will also be placed on DW.
Students on DW who commit another DW offense willbe
placed on Probation.
Students who commit an SW offense while on DW willbe
placed on extended DW.
Students who commit three (3) separate DW offensesin the
course of the year will be placed on Probation.
Students who commit four (4) separate DW offensesin the
course of the year may be sent to a Discipline Committee
Hearing or dismissed.
This recognizes that repeated rule violations areindicative of a more
serious problem. Students who attain DW in two consecutivemarking
terms may not receive a re-enrollment contract.
Probationary status may also be extended dependingupon student
behavior during the Probationary period. Studentswho commit an SW
or DW offense while on PRO will be placed on extendedPRO.
The Frederick Gunn School Student Handbook23
Seniors committing a Probationary offense within the last two weeks
prior to graduation or who are put on Probation for other reasons
during the last two weeks will be sent home and willnot be allowed
to participate in the graduation activities.

Students who commit a second Probationary offensewithin a year of
being removed from Probation (or who fail to meetattendance
requirements) will be subject to a Discipline CommitteeHearing (if not
separated from the school immediately). The DisciplineCommittee is
comprised of three Prefects and three members of thefaculty who are
appointed by the Dean of Students. The DisciplineCommittee Hearing
does not decide guilt; any student in a DisciplineCommittee Hearing
has already been found responsible for their behavior.At the
conclusion of the Hearing, the Discipline Committeewill make a
recommendation to the Head of School regarding a studentsfuture
at The Frederick Gunn School. The final decision willbe made by the
Head of School.

Any of the previously cited violations of conductlisted as major rule
violations may result in immediate dismissal fromthe school when the
seriousness of the offense warrants such decisiveaction. Such action
may be taken by the Head of School alone without involvementof the
Discipline Committee or Dean of Students.
As far as The Frederick Gunn School attempts to considereach
student as an individual, and each students disciplinarycase as an
individual case, students with similar (but not identical)disciplinary
offenses and records may occasionally merit differentresponses. In
the disposition of a major disciplinary case, thefollowing may be
taken into consideration: previous disciplinary record,contributions to
The Frederick Gunn School community beyond regularacademic and
athletic efforts, special home/family circumstances,and the impact of
the disciplinary offense upon the student, the studentbody, and the
faculty.
Students dismissed in the spring of senior year whocannot earn a
diploma at another educational institution may applyto receive a
Frederick Gunn diploma after successful completionof at least one
The Frederick Gunn School Student Handbook24
year of college. The diploma is not automatically conferred but may
be awarded after careful consideration of the studentsindividual
case history while at The Frederick Gunn School, circumstancesof the
dismissal, and college record.
Students separated from The Frederick Gunn Schoolmust have their
rooms cleaned out immediately and depart campus thatsame day.
Families must facilitate the retrieval and departureof their child
whether locally or from afar.

The school reserves the right to request at randomand with or without
cause the drug testing of any student by the Deanof Students in
consultation with the Head of School. Students arealso subject to a
drug test if found to be in possession of or are caughtusing an
E-Cigarette or vaporizer or suspiciously setting offany school fire
alarm.
Upon a failed first test, the student may be placedon Probation and
will discuss a cessation and/or recovery interventionwith the Director
of Health Services and Director of Counseling. Thestudent will be
tested again at random intervals for the durationof the Probationary
period. All drug testing will be at parental expense.Upon a repeated
failure of a drug test, a student may be requiredto appear before the
Discipline Committee. Students in possession of drugs,or other
substances used illegally and discovered as a resultof testing are also
subject to discipline, subsequent testing, and a possiblerequest for
professional intervention. Students who refuse drugtesting or tamper
with the test will have been considered to have failedthat test.
The Frederick Gunn School uses a zero-tolerance labto complete all
drug testing, and all samples are tested for a standardset of
intoxicants. The lab conducts confirmation tests onall positive results.
We will consider a student to have failed a drug testif they test
positive for any level of that drug (in other words,we do not rely on
federal minimum standards). In addition, a studentwill have failed a
drug test if they test positive for any substance(not just the substance
about which the school may have had a concern).
The Frederick Gunn School Student Handbook25

Sexual intimacy, while a normal and healthy aspectof adult life, is a
particularly complicated issue at a boarding schoolwhere we live as a
community given the living arrangements, the rangeof student ages,
and the diversity of values and beliefs for studentsand their families.
Furthermore, the School does not believe that mosthigh school
students are emotionally prepared for sex even, andperhaps
especially, given the increasing pressures of hookup culture and
pop-cultures portrayal of it as a purely physicalaffair. Therefore, the
School discourages sexual intimacy between studentson campus
and strictly prohibits sexual intimacy between adultsand students. We
endeavor, instead, to create an environment in whichstudents
become increasingly comfortable discussing the emotionaland
physical realities of sexual intimacy such that theyare prepared for
life. Additionally, concern for the emotional andphysical welfare of
Frederick Gunn School students is paramount and theSchool is
committed to helping students avoid sexually transmittedinfections,
pregnancy, and emotional complications that can accompanysexual
intimacy. Students with questions about these concernsshould go to
the Health Center, the Director of Counseling, theDean of Students, or
another trusted adult for guidance and resources.
Healthy romantic attachments do develop between students,and the
School seeks to support students as they search forappropriate ways
to express affection towards one another demonstratingrespect for
other members of the community. The School has equalexpectations
for all students regardless of their sexual orientation,and expects all
students involved in romantic relationships, whethersame or opposite
sex, to respect their partners privacy and the privacyof others.
Some sexually intimate behaviors may also violatestate laws
notwithstanding the consent of both parties. For example,sexual
contact with anyone three (3) years older when theother person is 13,
14, or 15 years of age is against Connecticut law.(SeeDefinition of
Statutory Rape in Sexual Misconduct Policy.) Sexualor emotional
intimacy between any student and any non-student adultmember of
The Frederick Gunn School community (e.g., employee,contractor,
The Frederick Gunn School Student Handbook27
vendor, volunteer, donor, parent) is strictly prohibited and against
School policy.

The State of Connecticut states that these classesare protected from
harassment: Age, ancestry, skin color, learning disability,marital
status, intellectual disability, national origin,physical disability, mental
disability, race, religious creed, sex, gender identityor expression,
sexual orientation, or any other protected class.Harassment, in this
context, is defined as any harmful conduct againsta person, or
persons, on the basis of their membership in a protectedclass. The
Frederick Gunn School does not tolerate harassmentin any form.

The Frederick Gunn School does not tolerate harassmentor
discrimination, and the school seeks to provide acommunity where
every individual is treated with respect and dignity.Transgressions of
this nature creates a hostile environment such thatthe conduct
unreasonably interferes with, limits, or denies anindividual
educational access or opportunities. Discriminationis defined as the
unfair or prejudicial treatment of people and groupsbased on the
protected classes mentioned in the above Harassmentsection.
Harassment or discrimination can be verbal (e.g. innuendos,threats,
ethnic slurs, derogatory jokes, pejorative epithets,propositions or
gestures), non-verbal (e.g. obscene gestures), written(including
online communications), visual (e.g graphic postersand drawings) or
physical (e.g unwanted touching, assault) that issevere or pervasive
and objectively offensive to the individual receivingthe harassing
behavior.

The school will not tolerate the use of bigoted languageor slurs by
anyone in our school community whether on campus,online via any
digital media, on school-related trips, off campus,at any
school-sponsored activities. Such slurs are offensiveand harmful to
individuals, erode the overall welfare of the FrederickGunn
community, and are considered a form of harassment.Slurs may be in
The Frederick Gunn School Student Handbook28
the form of verbal or written communications (which includes the use
of the n-word", anti-LGBT+ language, threats, derogatorycomments),
visible or heard gestures (which includes the Nazisalute, supremacist
hand signals, objectively divisive terms or phrasesin any language) or
visual symbols (which includes the Nazi swastika,racist paraphernalia,
and other insignia of oppression). In determiningwhether something
constitutes an identity-based slur, the school willconsider the
situation in which the slur was used and its historicalcontext of use,
with a focus on the detrimental impact of the sluron individuals and
on the environment of the school.
In order for the community to thrive, each individualmust feel a sense
of value and safety. According to the Frederick GunnSchools Core
Values, We are a school that nurtures Mr. Gunnsbelief in character as
the driving force in a life well-lived, and that characteremerges
through the intentional pursuit-in knowledge and practice-ofwhat is
good, right, true, sustainable, and beautiful. Wemust care deeply as
each individual practices treating others with respectand kindness,
and we must always be aware of the power of theirwords and actions
and the impressions on others that they create, whetherreal or
perceived.In these cases, claiming that one was kiddingor
joking will not be accepted as an excuse or justificationfor
inappropriate words or actions. If an individual reasonablyperceives
a students words or actions as disrespectful in anyway, that student
could be subject to The Frederick Gunn Schools formaldiscipline
system.
If you were involved in an instance of harassment,or observed a
form of harassment happening to a fellow communitymember (as
explained on previous pages), please reach out tothe Dean of
Students, Director of Counseling, the Director ofDiversity, Equity,
and Inclusion, your advisor, a trusted adult, or aPrefect.

Bullying is physical or verbal assault directed towardsa student or
group. Bullying generally is defined as the repeateduse by one or
more students of a written, verbal or electronic expression(such as
cyber-bullying) or a physical act or gesture or anycombination
thereof, directed at a victim that: (i) causes physicalor emotional
The Frederick Gunn School Student Handbook29
harm to the victim or damage to the victims property; (ii) places the
victim in reasonable fear of harm to himself/herselfor of damage to
their property;( iii) creates a hostile environmentat school for the
victim; (iv) infringes on the rights of the victimat school; or (v)
materially and substantially disrupts the educationprocess or the
orderly operation of a school.
Please note that a hostile environment exists whenconduct is
sufficiently severe or pervasive that it materiallyinterferes with a
students educational experience. See policies onHarassment and
Discrimination, and Sexual Misconduct.
Cyber-bullying generally is defined as bullying throughthe use of
technology or any electronic communication, whichshall include, but
shall not be limited to, any transfer of signs, signals,writing, images,
sounds, data or intelligence of any nature transmittedin whole or in
part by a wire, radio, electromagnetic, photo electronicor photo
optical system, including, but not limited to, electronicmail, internet
communications, instant messages or facsimile communications.
Cyber-bullying shall also include (i) the creationof a web page or
blog in which the creator assumes the identity ofanother person or (ii)
the knowing impersonation of another person as theauthor of posted
content or messages, if the creation or impersonationcreates any of
the conditions enumerated in clauses (i) to (v), inclusive,of the
definition of bullying. Cyber-bullying shall alsoinclude the distribution
by electronic means of a communication to more thanone person or
the posting of material on an electronic medium thatmay be
accessed by one or more persons, if the distributionor posting creates
any of the conditions enumerated in clauses (i) to(v), inclusive, of the
definition of bullying.
Hazing is the exertion of pressure, intimidation,or force (whether
physical or verbal) on a particular student or groupto perform
humiliating, demeaning, or dangerous tasks. The FrederickGunn
School prides itself on being a close-knit community.By definition,
bullying (including cyberbullying) and hazing areforms of harassment
and will not be tolerated. Forms of bullying, hazing,or any other forms
of harassment including, for example, posting derogatorycomments
of any Frederick Gunn School student, faculty member,or employee
on social network sites such as Facebook, Instagram,Twitter, YouTube,
The Frederick Gunn School Student Handbook30
etc. are subject to the most severe levels of discipline, including
Probation.
Any student who feels that they or any other studenthas been the
victim of an action of bullying (including cyber bullying),hazing or
retaliation is strongly encouraged to report the matterpromptly to the
Dean of Students or the Head of School. Student reportsof bullying,
hazing or retaliation may be made anonymously. TheSchool prohibits
retaliation against any person who in good faith reportsany incident
of bullying (including cyberbullying) or hazing, whoprovides
information during an investigation, or who witnessesor has reliable
information pertaining to bullying or hazing. Retaliationmeans any
form of intimidation or harassment directed againstany such person.
A student who recklessly and maliciously makes a falseaccusation of
bullying, hazing or retaliation will be subject todisciplinary action, up
to and including dismissal.
Once any allegation of bullying, hazing or retaliationis received, an
investigation of the charge will be conducted by theSchool.

Testing: In September, a SARS-CoV2 (COVID-19) PCRtest is required
to be done 72 hours prior to their arrival on campus. To gain access to
campus the result must be negative. The results willbe uploaded to
their Magnus Health Account prior to their arrivalof campus
All students and employees will be tested as recommendedby the
State of CT DPH guidelines with a COVID-19 PCR test.
Weekly, random surveillance COVID-19 PCR testing willoccur following
the CT DPH guidelines until the students go home inNovember.
Students presenting to the health center with COVID-19symptoms, per
CDC guidelines; (Fever or chills, cough, shortnessof breath or difficulty
breathing, fatigue, muscle or body aches, headache,new loss of taste
or smell, sore throat, congestion or runny nose, nauseaor vomiting
and/or diarrhea, overly fatigued) will receive anAbbott ID NOW rapid
test at the Health Center. If this test is positivethe student will be
isolated, contact tracing will begin, and the parent/guardianwill be
notified and asked to pick up their child within 12hours for the entire
duration of isolation.
Quarantine: Those students found to have been closecontacts of a
suspected COVID-19 student or a student found to bepositive for
COVID-19 through testing will be placed in quarantinefor 10-14 days,
The Frederick Gunn School Student Handbook60
unless fully vaccinated, per CDC guidelines. During this period they
will be quarantined either in their dorm room withtheir cohort and
roommates, or moved to another dorm designated forquarantining.
We encourage parents/guardians to take their studentshome during
this lengthy period. The students will be observedfor the possible
development of any COVID-19 symptoms, discussed above.If
symptoms develop, the student will be isolated, testedfor COVID-19
with a RT-PCR test and sent home.While in quarantine,the students
will remain in their room with the door closed, mealswill be delivered
to their dorm room, and scheduled periods of outdooractivity will be
arranged, and monitored.
Isolation: A student found to be positive for COVID-19through RT-PCR
testing or to display symptoms consistent with COVID-19,discussed
above, will be placed in isolation. The isolationunit is situated in the
Memorial Building, above the Health Center. The studentwill be placed
in a private room, where meals will be delivered tothem.
Parents/guardians are expected to pick up their studentwithin 12
hours. A RT-PCR test will be performed on the studentprior to their
departure.
For most students with COVID-19 isolation may be discontinued10
days after symptom onset and resolution of fever forat least 24 hours,
without the use of fever-reducing medications, andwith improvement
of other symptoms. For students who never developsymptoms,
isolation and other precautions can be discontinued10 days after the
date of their first positive RT-PCR test for SARS-CoV-2RNA.
All students returning to school following a COVID-19illness must be
cleared through the health center, either via zoomor a phone
assessment.

Medical leave applies to all students who are physicallyor
psychologically unable to meet Frederick Gunn Schoolexpectations
and/or be at The Frederick Gunn School due to a diagnosedmedical
condition, mental health condition, and/or an emergencyoperation or
accident for an extended period of time. The FrederickGunn School, in
consultation with medical professionals, determineswhether a
student is eligible for Medical Leave when and ifa student may return
The Frederick Gunn School Student Handbook61
from Medical Leave. In addition, students who go on Medical Leave
concurrent with a disciplinary situation may stillface disciplinary
consequences if they are allowed to return to campus.
If, while at home on leave, the students medicalcondition permits
them to keep up with schoolwork, they will do so fromhome, given
medical limitations. Medical documentation will guidethe school in
making this decision. No tests will be administeredduring this time,
but other non-proctored forms of assessment may berequired. The
Academic office will decide what work must be completedby the
student and will coordinate with faculty to send andcollect work to
and from students. Whatever work the student has notcompleted at
home will be done once the student has returned toschool and at a
pace deemed reasonable by the teacher in consultationwith the
Academic office and the student. If, while at homeon leave, the
student is found by the medical authority to be incapableof doing
schoolwork, The Frederick Gunn School will determinenext steps.
Students designated to be on medical leave will automaticallymove
to a No Credit/Credit grading system while on leave.When the
duration of a medical leave is less than half a term,grades will revert
to the Frederick Gunn School grading system upon thestudents return
to school. When a medical leave extends to more thanhalf a term,
the No Credit/Credit will remain and will be reflectedon their official
transcript with the notation of Off Campus. Shouldthe medical leave
extend beyond one term, the school will consult withthe student and
family about next steps, which will likely includea requirement to
repeat the academic year and/or withdraw. Any workdone through a
third-party institution will be documented on thatinstitutions
transcript and will be appended to the students FrederickGunn
School record.
The Dean of Students, in consultation with the Headof School, Director
of Counseling, and other medical professionals, willoutline the
conditions of a medical leave and any additional actionsthat must be
completed during the leave. A student must completethese actions in
order to be considered for return to the school. Failureto complete
these actions will lead to a required withdrawal fromschool. While The
Frederick Gunn School will consult with medical professionals,it is
ultimately the decision of the school whether or nota student may
The Frederick Gunn School Student Handbook62
return to campus. Considerations include, but are not limited to, the
students adherence to the conditions of the leave,how long they were
off campus, the amount of academic work completed,and the
students influence within the community.

The Frederick Gunn School uses the term co-curricularto refer to
adult-led student activities that typically occurafter or outside of the
class day. These activities can include performingand visual arts,
athletics, Community Service, and other programs suchas Outdoor
Club, and certain Independent Projects. The term replacesthe
extra-curricular or the after school program toreflect The Frederick
Gunn Schools belief that nearly every part of lifeat a boarding school
is an opportunity for teaching and learning and thereforepart of the
curriculum.Students are required to participate ina co-curricular
activity every term. Beyond that, students are requiredto participate
in a minimum of two (2) terms of an interscholasticathletic team in
their first year and a minimum of one (1) term ineach successive
year.
While this policy gives flexibility to students, theschool continues to
believe that a variety of experiences is valuable.With that in mind,
students may not concentrate their afternoons towardsa singular
activity for all three terms of the year. For example,a student who does
a fitness option (X- term or an equivalent) in thefall in preparation for
the winter basketball season may not do a similarfitness option in the
spring. Similarly, a student who rows crew in thefall and the spring
may not weight train for crew in the winter.
The Frederick Gunn School recognizes that studentsinterests may not
always be met by the schools formal on-campus co-curricular
offerings. As such, students are encouraged to investigateand pursue
independent projects that further their developmentin an area of
interest. Such projects may be through organizationsaffiliated with
The Frederick Gunn School or with third parties. AllIndependent
Projects must be approved by the Director of Co-Curricularsand the
appropriate Program Director (Athletic Director, VisualArts Chair,
Performing Arts Chair, etc.). While engaged in anIndependent
The Frederick Gunn School Student Handbook63
Co-Curricular Project, students (new or returning) must continue to
meet the policy requirements stated above. Independent
Co-Curricular Projects should reinforce the Core Valuesof The
Frederick Gunn Schools co-curricular program as identifiedin this
policy.
Fulfilling The Frederick Gunn Schools co-curricularrequirements is
necessary to receive a diploma upon graduation. Studentswho are
unable to meet the requirements of the schools policyfor medical
reasons will be granted an exemption. Families willneed to provide
documentation of the rationale for exemption froma doctor. Other
exemptions, if any, will be granted only by the Headof School.

The Frederick Gunn School has a College Counselingstaff consisting
of one Director of College Counseling, one Associateof College
Counseling, two College Counselors, and a full-timeAdministrative
Assistant. The College Counseling staff meets withsophomores,
juniors and seniors periodically throughout the academicyear.
Complete information regarding the college applicationprocess and
College Counseling curriculum can be found in theCollege
Counseling Handbook.

The junior spring and senior fall are pivotal timesduring which
students need to be focused on academics and shouldnot miss
school. As such, the College Counseling Office stronglyurges students
and families to conduct college visits during summersand Frederick
Gunn School vacations. For unforeseen or unavoidablecollege visits,
seniors are permitted to be off campus for two daysin the fall term.
Should it be necessary, seniors are permitted to beoff campus for two
additional days in the spring for the purpose of collegerevisit days.
Juniors are expected to limit their college visitsin the fall and winter to
times when The Frederick Gunn School is on vacation.Both Spring
Break and the Spring Heads Weekend provide excellentopportunities
for juniors to visit colleges. For unavoidable absences,juniors are
permitted two days in the spring term for the purposesof college
visits. All college related absences must be clearedthrough the Dean
The Frederick Gunn School Student Handbook64
of Students Office by completing a time off-campus (TOC) form which
requires approval of the College Counselor, AcademicOffice, and
Dean of Students. College visit days are to be usedonly for the
purpose of scheduled college appointments and aregiven to students
during the first two weeks of each term. Studentsare expected to plan
their visits ahead of time and failure to do so mayresult in detention.
Last minute requests should be brought to the Deanof Students Office
and the College Counseling Office.

Students are expected to disclose all pertinent informationon their
college applications. If a college application asksspecific questions
about discipline, it is the students responsibilityto respond honestly. If
there is a change in the disciplinary status of asenior that results in
temporary or permanent separation from the schoolor if a student
voluntarily withdraws from school prior to graduation,the student
must notify the colleges to which they have appliedwithin two weeks
of the date of the change in status. At the end ofthis two-week period
or one week prior to graduation, whichever comes first,the College
Counseling Office will notify colleges in writingof the change in status.
Should the College Counseling Office be asked forverification
regarding discipline, separation, or withdrawal, theschool will confirm
the student report, but will refer the college backto the student/ family
for further details.
If a student is found responsible for sexual misconductand is
dismissed, the School will not recommend the studentto another high
school, college, university, or potential employer(see Note below). In
this event, even if no Release of Information formhas been completed
for the student, any institution that has recentlyrequested and/or is
requesting the students transcript will be informedthat the student
was found responsible for sexual misconduct and dismissed.
Note:If a student under disciplinary investigationfor sexual
misconduct withdraws, the investigation and adjudicationprocess will
nevertheless be completed. Should that student befound responsible,
and even if no Release of Information form is completed,any
institution that has recently requested and/or isrequesting the
The Frederick Gunn School Student Handbook65
students transcript will be informed of the result of the investigation
and adjudication process.

The following provisions have been added to the Student Handbook in
regards to compliance with the global pandemic ofCOVID-19. The
terms and guidelines set forth in this Handbook maycontinue to be
modified as the school year progresses due to CDCand State of
Connecticut regulations and modifications.
The health and safety of our community is the toppriority of The
Frederick Gunn School. Many of the items below representbasic daily
behaviors that it is incumbent on all members of thecommunity to
abide by, aware that personal daily habit formationand responsibility
is, as usual, the best path to a successful year foreveryone.
In correspondence with CDC and State of Connecticutguidelines and
best practices, all students will be required to betested for COVID-19
3-5 days before returning to campus. Additionally,students and their
families will be required to read and sign the SocialContract,
designating that they understand and comply with thepolicies set
forth by The Frederick Gunn School.
The school will also engage in contract tracing ifthere is a suspected
positive COVID-19 case to safeguard the communityshealth. Students
are expected to participate fully in COVID-19 testingand contract
tracing, answering their questions honestly and completely.
We understand that these policies are still new tothe community, and
as such, there will be education of the guidelinesduring Student
Orientation and multiple times throughout the year.Students will be
reminded by the community to follow and comply withthe guidelines
frequently, as it will help keep our community safeand allow us to
remain on-campus.
If a student does not comply with the health and safetymeasures
presented by The Frederick Gunn School, communitymembers will
communicate with the student directly and the Deanof Students
Office, where they will track offenses. Should theoffenses occur in a
habitual manner, students will receive a formal anddocumented
communication from the Dean of Students Office.
Should a student continue to fail to comply with theguidelines
presented in the Student Handbook and Social Contract,the student

The student should understand that if they continueto fail to comply

I am really hoping that this internship will allow me to see what strategies a new and developing company
uses to effectively attract new buyers. I also want to potentially help apply new marketing avenues.
Going into this internship without prior professional marketing experience, I hope to find out if I want to
pursue marketing alongside chemistry or product development as a possible career path. I am looking
forward to working in a lab and getting to experience research as a profession related to chemistry.

Ever since sixth grade, chemistry has intrigued me, especially getting to see how everything is composed
of chemical elements. Taking AP chemistry really challenged me to think how chemistry impacts our
everyday lives. I began to see chemistry in everything from icy-hot to mustard packets to pool water.
Helping prepare labs with my chemistry teachers once per week remains a highlight, and I am super
excited to work in a laboratory for longer time periods through this experience. I love thinking about the
molecular interactions and understanding chemistry behind products. I knew I wanted to pursue a senior
project with chemistry as the main component, and probably pursue a career involving chemistry.
I knew solitary research was probably not for me, especially if I would be in a lab with minimal interaction
with others. So I wanted to make sure that I could learn from others and interact as a part of a new project
and group of people on a daily basis. The dilemma of wanting to pursue chemistry without being in a
laboratory made me think about where I could go for my senior project. I realized I have such a passion
for people and art and ethics! I have fund raised over 5,500 in the past two years for two different
organizations and marketing was integral to raising this money. I absolutely loved crafting social media
posts and sending out hand-designed letters. As one individual raising this money, these methods were
effective and efficient enough, but I would like to see how companies invest their time and resources into
marketing, because marketing would be an amazing field to enter into. Getting to work in a laboratory
on product development as well, will combine my love for chemistry with art and ethics.

This course introduces the broad science of psychology from both the natural science and
social science perspectives. Weekly lessons are combined with small group seminar discus-
sions to provide the opportunity for exploring how the scientific method has been applied to
the challenge of understanding human developmental changes and individual differences in
thought, feeling, and behavior. Topics include biological bases of behavior, sensory and per-
ceptual processes, learning, motivation, emotion, personality, maturational and develop-
mental changes, individual differences, social behavior, clinical and abnormal psychology. By
the end of the course, students will have an appreciation for the history and current status
of cognitive, developmental, social, and clinical psychology.

These college-level courses introduce students to the principles that apply to the individuals,
their decision-making, the world, and the economic system as a whole. This course helps
them to understand how the world functions, how prices are determined, how markets
function, how markets fail, the role that the government plays, how currencies are valued,
financial sector basics, stabilization policies, why some countries are more developed than
others, economic growth and international economics. Students learn to use graphs, charts,
and data to analyze, describe and explain economic concepts, and think like economists.

content:
This is an introductory college-level statistics course that introduces students to the major
concepts and tools for collecting, analyzing, and drawing conclusions from data. Students
cultivate their understanding of statistics using technology, investigations, problem-solving,
and writing as they explore concepts like variation and distribution; patterns and uncertain-
ty; and data-based predictions, decisions, and conclusions.

Explore how humans have understood, used, and changed the surface of Earth. Students will
use the tools and thinking processes of geographers to examine patterns of human popula-
tion, migration, and land use. Students will learn skills such as: connecting geographic con-
cepts and processes to real-life scenarios; understanding information shown in maps, tables,
charts, graphs, infographics, images, and landscapes; seeing patterns and trends in data and
in visual sources such as maps and drawing conclusions from them; and understanding spa-
tial relationships using geographic scales. Topics include: population and migration, cultural
and political patterns, agriculture and rural and urban land use processes, and economic and
industrial development.

metadata.parent_section: 4. AP Human Geography / AP 人文地理:

content:
In this introductory course, students will learn to design and evaluate solutions and apply
computer science to solve problems through the development of algorithms and programs.
They will incorporate abstraction into programs and use data to discover new knowledge.
Students will also explain how computing innovations and computing systems, including the
Internet, work, explore their potential impacts and contribute to a computing culture that is
collaborative and ethical.

metadata.parent_section: 5. AP Computer Science Principles / AP 计算机科学原理:

content:
This course introduces students to computer science through programming. Fundamental
topics in this course include the design of solutions to problems, the use of data structures
to organize large sets of data, the development and implementation of algorithms to pro-
cess data and discover new information, the analysis of potential solutions, and the ethical
and social implications of computing systems. The course emphasizes object-oriented pro-
gramming and design using the Java programming language (College Board, 2019). Instruc-
tion includes preparation for the AP Computer Science A Exam.

metadata.parent_section: 6. AP Computer Science A / AP 计算机科学 A:

content:
Develop your 2-D through materials and processes such as graphic design, photography,
collage, printmaking, fashion illustration, collage, and others. You'll create artwork that
reflects your own ideas and skills and what you've learned.

metadata.parent_section: 7. AP 2-D Art and Design / AP 2-D 艺术及设计

content:
An introductory college-level drawing course. Students refine and apply drawing skills to
ideas they develop throughout the course.

Develop 3-D skills in materials and processes, such as sculpture, architectural rendering and
models, metalwork, ceramics, glasswork, and others. You'll create artwork that reflects your
own ideas and skills and what youve learned.

The AP Music Theory course corresponds to one-to-two semesters of typical, introductory
college music theory coursework that covers topics such as musicianship, theory, and musi-
cal materials and procedures. Musicianship skills, including dictation and listening skills,
sight-singing, and harmony, are an important part of the course. Through the course, stu-
dents develop the ability to recognize, understand, and describe basic materials and pro-
cesses of tonal music that are heard or presented in a score. The development of aural
(listening) skills is a primary objective. Performance is also part of the curriculum through
the practice of sight-singing. Students learn basic concepts and terminology by listening to
and performing a wide variety of music. Notational skills, speed, and fluency with basic ma-
terials are emphasized.
Art Electives / 艺术类课程选修课

metadata.parent_section: 10. AP Music Theory / AP 乐理:

content:
What does it mean to be a good writer? How do we know, and can therefore produce, good
writing, be it fiction, poetry, or non-fiction essay? In this elective creative writing course, we
will read and discuss literary work and essays that deal with a multitude of human experi-
ences, study writing as a craft, and write original creative stories and critical essays. Lectures
are combined with writing workshops, for which students will receive constructive feedback
on their creative and critical work.

This elective course will provide violin, viola, cello, and double bass students with challeng-
ing and varied repertoire while also studying music history and theory concepts. Students
will work as an ensemble to continue developing their music skills, including posture, tone,
technique, intonation, articulation, dynamics, blend, balance, expression, and overall musi-
cianship. Students will study some music theory concepts such as written theory, aural skills,
and composition. Music history will be explored through learning about composers and lis-
tening to major musical works from various style periods. Students will need to have
knowledge of sight-reading and the ability to play an instrument to ABRSM grade 5 or equiv-
alent.

This elective course will provide students with challenging and varied methods of expressing
ideas and concepts through digital media. Students will work as individuals and in small pro-
duction teams to continue to develop their research, design, and digital media production
skills by exploring a wide range of current topics and sources. Students will develop a highly
accomplished and sophisticated ability to review and refine ideas as their work develops,
demonstrating an analytical and critical understanding through mature referencing of feed-
back and self-reflection. Students will produce digital media content, realizing initial design
intentions accomplished by making connections between digital and design elements to
create a personal digital response.

The course provides students the opportunity to develop the skills required to create digital
art pieces using the international leading standard software ADOBE, focusing on the genera-
tion of ideas. The course will enhance the creative process by aiding the traditional mark-
making procedure with the use of the software, which is used worldwide in several indus-
tries, including but not limited to fashion, arts, design, photography, visual production, archi-
tecture, among others.

metadata.parent_section: 14. Digital Art & Photography / 数字艺术与摄影:

content:
This course is open to instrumentalists and vocalists who want to perform a variety of chal-
lenging repertoire from the Jazz idiom and beyond. We will listen to and analyze iconic re-
cordings, learning about their historical context and relevant stylistic conventions. We will
also learn to apply music theory concepts as creators through improvisation and composi-
tion.

In this elective course, students will investigate and develop 2-D art making skills. Students
will explore traditional and contemporary methods of art-making, incorporating various
media. The course will focus heavily on the works of contemporary artists but will refer-
ence historical art pieces. In addition, the class will follow thematic threads woven through
time and cultures. This course is based upon the quality of individual expression, a thor-
ough knowledge of historical perspective, and an understanding of current trends, with art
as a vehicle of communication.

metadata.parent_section: 16. Art 2-D/Advanced Art 2-D / 2-D 艺术、高阶 2-D 艺术:

content:
Develop 3-D skills in materials and processes, such as sculpture, architectural rendering and
models, metalwork, ceramics, glasswork, and others. You'll create artwork that reflects
your own ideas and skills and what you've learned.

metadata.parent_section: 17. Art 3-D/Advanced 3-D / 3-D 艺术、高阶 3-D 艺术

content:
Print media is a critical practice grounded in the history of all printed matter and the print-
ed form as a social medium. Students will participate in a comprehensive range of technical
and aesthetic approaches centered on a range of strategies, including the artwork as multi-
ple, digital, and cultural production.

This course will provide singers with a challenging and varied repertoire while also studying
music history and theory concepts. Students will work as an ensemble to continue develop-
ing their musical skills, including proper vocal technique, posture, breathing, tone, intona-
tion, diction, dynamics, expression, and overall musicianship. Music theory concepts to be
studied include written theory, aural skills, sight-singing, and composition. Music history
will be explored through learning about composers and listening to major musical works
from various style periods. Students will work to achieve musical goals as a group and as
individuals, building a foundation for future musical experiences, whether as a performer
or audience members. This course meets the UC A-G criteria for a Visual and Fine Arts cred-
it.

This course is an introduction to the craft of acting. Students learn theory and practice of
acting through exercises, rehearsals, and games, improving their ability to concentrate,
relax, listen, observe and practice empathy.

Learn how to write, produce, record, mix and master your own songs from start to finish.
Learn to write melodies, lyrics, and chord progressions. Learn how to structure your songs
by understanding the function of a verse, pre-chorus, chorus, bridge, post-chorus, intro,
and outro. Learn to record and edit MIDI and audio using Apples Logic Pro X software
along with music production hardware. Learn the art of sound design, beat production,
synthesis, layering, orchestration, vocal comping, and pitch correction. Learn the secrets of
mixing and mastering, including effectively using EQ, compression, reverb, automation,
saturation, stereo imaging, ear candy, and other processes to prepare your tracks for re-
lease.

content:
This course introduces students to advanced Latin grammar, vocabulary, and syntax. Stu-
dents continue to learn new verb and pronoun forms, as well as increased varieties of case
usage, while Latin texts continue to be significantly adapted. By the end of the year, stu-
dents approach readiness to read near-authentic Latin with significant lexical assistance.
Through Latin stories as well as English-language secondary sources, students learn about
the city of Rome: its most famous buildings and the governmental structures housed
there.

This is a first-year Spanish course with equal emphasis on the four basic skills of compre-
hension: listening, speaking, reading, and writing. Students will acquire knowledge in Span-
ish by continually increasing their vocabulary, grammar, and use of idiomatic expressions.
Students will learn to write short sentences in the present tense on various topics. Stu-
dents will describe, ask and answer questions, engage in simple conversations, and carry
out simple, realistic functions to communicate in the target language.

This is an intermediate Spanish course with equal emphasis on the three major modes of
communication: interpretive (reading and listening), interpersonal (writing and speaking),
and presentational (writing and speaking). Students will acquire knowledge in Spanish by
continually increasing their vocabulary, grammar, and use of idiomatic expressions. Stu-
dents will practice speaking and writing short sentences in the present, present progres-
sive, and preterit tenses on various topics. Students will describe, ask and answer ques-
tions, engage in simple conversations, and carry out simple, realistic functions to com-
municate in the target language. Students will be assessed in a variety of ways, including
exams and quizzes, essays, presentations, role-plays, skits, and other projects.

This course will explore the various global political institutions and their merits, with a
specific focus on the United Nations and its various organs. Moreover, the course has a
major focus on simulating the later organization, and thus it will develop debate, speaking,
research, argumentative, and evidently critical thinking skills.

metadata.parent_section: 25. Global Politics and Development / 全球政治与发展:

content:
In Speech and Debate, students will learn how to write, organize, prepare, and deliver
quality public speeches. Students will study how to actively persuade, inspire, inform, and
engage an audience through the art of public speaking. We will begin by studying the fun-
damentals of public communication.

metadata.parent_section: 26. Speech and Debate / 演讲与辩论:

content:
This is an entry-level course for students who want to learn the basics of business and man-
agement in an interesting way. The course teaches students some basic entrepreneurial
skills while allowing them to explore their understanding of marketing, advertising, human
resources, financial management, and operations through a project-based learning ap-
proach. This course aims to support and develop students creativity, problem-solving skills,
teamwork, leadership skills, confidence, and language skills while giving them an opportuni-
ty to build their thoughts and ideas about the business into something neat and concrete.
The course also helps to prepare students for participating in internationally recognized
business stimulations and competitions.

metadata.parent_section: 27. Business Innovation and Entrepreneurship / 商业创新与创业:

content:
The elective course in Geology is intended to introduce the student to the general princi-
ples of geology and its importance as a science. Topics will be entirely dictated by the stu-
dents own research and interests but could include physical geology, geophysics, disaster
prediction and management, paleontology, mineral exploration and extraction, building
planning, and any other geological field students find of interest or value to their further
studies. The course will be taught by a series of lessons, laboratories, and project-based
work that will be carried out both independently and in small groups. By the end of the
course, students will have an appreciation for the importance of the field of geology to
human development, how life developed, and the implications for the future of life on
earth.

The class is designed to be both challenging and engaging, where students will learn and
apply the components of physical fitness to their studies. Students will gain exposure to an
array of sports, both domestic and abroad, and will assess the skills needed, the rules, and
the enjoyment of the sport. The expectations for athletes in this course are to have fun,
challenge themselves and their peers, and carry a professional attitude on and off the field
of play.

Sustainability science is the study of the dynamic relationship between humans and the
environment, particularly focusing on the vulnerability, robustness, resilience, and stability
of the coupled human-environment system. This course provides an interdisciplinary explo-
ration of the major challenges that sustainable development seeks to address, for example,
population growth; energy, food, and water supply; and urban and economic development.

metadata.source_file: 附件3：Introduction of 2023 BIBS · C Team Recruitment of iGEM.pdf

content:
The International Genetically Engineered Machine (iGEM) is an international science
and technology competition dedicated to the advancement of synthetic biology. It
involves interdisciplinary cooperation in mathematics, computing, statistics and other
fields. The competition and achievements of iGEM are featured by top academic
magazines such as Science, Nature, Scientific American, The Economist and traditional
media such as BBC, which has gained wide international influence.
国际基因工程机器大赛，英文名称为International Genetically Engineered Machine
competition，简称 iGEM，是合成生物学领域的国际顶级科技赛事，也是涉及数
学、计算机、统计学等领域交叉合作的跨学科竞赛。国际基因工程机器大赛赛况
和研究成果每年都受到《科学》、《自然》、《科学美国人》、《经济学人》等
顶级学术杂志、英国广播公司这样的传统媒体的关注并进行专题报道，具有广泛
的国际影响力。

metadata.source_file: 附件3：Introduction of 2023 BIBS · C Team Recruitment of iGEM.pdf

content:
Students who have a solid foundation in biology, mathematics, computer science,
statistics, business studies, chemistry and even the arts are welcome to work on the
project. A team consists of 12-20 members. The competition period of IGEM lasts for
almost one year. Registration begins in March every year and ends on June, while the
on-site presentation will be attended at the end of October. iGEM will officially check
whether they are qualified for the final. Once qualified, the team will send
representatives to defend, and the judges will conduct multiple rounds of selection to
evaluate the prize.
生物、数学、计算机、统计学、商科、化学甚至艺术等学科基础扎实的学生，均
可在项目中承担相应的工作。一支队伍由 12-20 人组成。iGEM 通常需要持续一
年的学习。每年3月开始报名，6月1日队伍报名截止，10月底参加答辩。iGEM
官方审核是否具有参加决赛的资格，获取资格后，团队中派出代表进行答辩，评
委将进行多轮筛选进行评奖。

content:
BIBS · C iGEM team will take marine microorganism as the research object to conduct
basic research on marine microorganism system and synthetic biology. Marine
microorganism cultured in large quantities by biotechnology can generate high value
in medicine, food, environment, renewable energy and other fields. In order to deal
with the issue of environmental protection, the molecular mechanism of the marine
microorganism genome sequence will be studied through artificial intelligence,
genome editing, bioinformatics and other technologies. Thus, a carbon-free marine
1 / 6
microorganism project can be formed in different environments to regenerate clean
energy.
中国·贝赛思iGEM 战队将以海洋微生物作为研究对象，进行海洋微生物系统和合
成生物学基础研究和成果转化。应用生物技术进行大量培养或生产的海洋微生物
能在医药、食品、动物饲料、环境检测、净化环境、生物技术、可再生能源等领
域产生极高的附加值。该项目将通过人工智能、基因组编辑、生物信息学等技术，
对海洋微生物基因组序列的分子机理进行研究，使得在不同环境下可以形成一个
完整的物质和能量循环利用的闭环零碳或负碳海洋微生物的项目，以应对社会环
境保护问题。

Project Introduction of Long-term Research Program
长期科研学习项目课程简介
Project 1: Survey of plankton community of the coastal environment of Shenzhen
项目一：深圳周边海域浮游生物生态调查
Phytoplankton are the primary producer and the key oxygen producer in the aquatic
environment. They form the basis of the food web; They are considered important
proxy to environmental pollution; They play an important role in the geochemical
cycles of important elements. This project focuses on the seasonal variation and
spatial distribution of phytoplankton in the coastal environment of ShenZhen.
Sampling of phytoplankton will be conducted quarterly. Phytoplankton species will be
observed under light microscope and the image data will be used to establish a training
data set for automated identification by AI. A database of phytoplankton as well as
their occurrence pattern will be analyzed and linked with environmental parameters,
through which the project aims at (1) facilitate automated identification of
phytoplankton specimens collected in Shen Zhen and (2) provide the foundation for
future modeling of environmental events such as harmful algal bloom (3) establish the
biodiversity and ecosystem health index of Shen Zhen coastal environment.

供应者，它启动了水域生态系统中的食物网，在水域生态系统的能量流动、物质

Project 2: Study of phototaxis in the larvae of marine benthos
项目二：海洋浮游-底栖生物趋光性研究
Benthic organisms is a crucial part in the marine ecosystem. Bryozoans are a group of
marine benthos that have an indispensable role in maintaining marine biodiversity but
are least known by the public. From the coastal water to 5500m in the deep sea, and
from the equator to the polar seas, bryozoans are highly successful in colonizing
different habitats. They grow and cover biotic or abiotic surfaces, and hence they
possess severe biofouling problem to other sessile marine invertebrates as well as to
the mankind. Up-to-date, little is known about their larval settlement mechanism,
especially how their response to light facilitate the choice of settling substrate. This
project aims at developing auto tracking algorithm for automated recording and
analysis of bryozoans' larval phototactic response. The project involved both wet lab
and dry lab computational experiments to capture and analyze some unknown larval
behavior.

Project 3: Study of the Feeding behavior of Marine flatworms
项目三：海洋底栖生物摄食研究
Flatworms, or Platyhelminthes, are of great significance in the evolution of animals, as
its emergence is a huge leap in the history of evolution. It marks the transition from
the aquatic to terrestrial environments, and from fixed/floating to free-living crawling
lifeforms. Because of its strong regeneration power, platyhelminthes are good model
for studying molecular mechanism of cell differentiation, dedifferentiation, animal
behavior and chromosome. This project will deploy the infrared imaging tracking
equipment (developed by ourselves), and will use the AI machine vision technology to
study the feeding behavior of this group of animals.
选择扁形动物作为研究对象，在动物的进化中具有重要意义。扁形动物的出现，
是动物发展史上一次质的飞跃，它标志着动物界的演化发展已开始由水生向陆生、
由固着或漂浮生活向自由爬行生活过渡。由于扁形动物的再生能力特别强，因而
又是研究细胞分化与去分化分子机理和动物行为及染色体的好材料，一直是动物
界热衷探索的研究领域。本项目运用自行研发的红外成像追踪设备，利用人工智
能机器视觉技术，深度研究其摄食行为。

The IB Diploma Programme (IBDP) is a rigorous, academically challenging and balanced Programme of
education designed to prepare students aged 16 to 19 for success at university and life beyond. The DP
aims to encourage students to be knowledgeable, inquiring, caring and compassionate, and to develop
intercultural understanding, open-mindedness, and the attitudes necessary to respect and evaluate a
range of viewpoints.

Online Courses Through Pamoja
Pamoja, in collaboration with the IB, offers various IB courses online at different levels. Courses are
taught by experienced IB teachers from around the world. Students take classes in groups of 10 or fewer
with classmates from around the world. As many educational institutions are exploring the world of
online learning, Pamoja gives our students access to the forefront of educational innovations. Pamoja
also allows for more individualized learning opportunities for students with various strengths or
interests.

organized and good at managing their time. The Pamoja schedule does not always follow Qibao
Dwights schedule so students will often need to complete assignments even during Chinese National
Holidays. Assignments are given on a weekly basis and due each Tuesday evening. A week usually
consists of one larger tasks and a few smaller tasks. Students are expected to spend roughly 5-6 hours
per week on their courses. Students who wish to take an online course must first get permission from

Applications to switch courses or levels will be reviewed by the DP Coordinator and Curriculum
Director. Decisions will be based on:
- Impact on overall schedule (space in classes, number of classes and teachers that need to switch,
etc..)
- Students must have fulfilled any pre-requisite in G10 for any HL class they want to switch into
(i.e. if the student wants to switch from Chemistry SL to HL but only got a 4 in G10 chemistry,
the request would be denied)
- In order to switch into an HL, the head of the department for that subject must approve your
switch. This may require students to complete a set task over the October holiday. (Only for
application in the first month)

Students must be aware that students may be co-sat (HL and SL students in the same classroom) in
order to accommodate a switch. This is quite common in IB schools, especially in certain subject
groups.

时光荏苒，白驹过隙，又到了欢笑与泪水齐飞的毕业季。学校特此发布2018届毕业生大学录取情
况，与师生家长共享喜悦。我们由衷感谢三年来全体师生的共同努力！你们每一个人都是七德独一无二
的骄傲！祝贺大家！
截至2018年4月2日，据不完全统计，七宝德怀特12年级毕业生149人共收到来自8个国家与地区的
总计近600份offer。斩获美国常春藤及新常春藤名校20所。九成以上的学生拿到了至少一个全美排
名前50的综合性大学/文理学院/艺术院校、英国排名前20大学、加拿大排名前5大学、澳大利亚排名前3
大学，累计奖学金近300万美金！
相比2017届，我们又有了新的突破：一是收获了世界顶尖名校约翰霍普金斯大学、西北大学、莱
斯大学、圣母大学、华盛顿圣路易斯、弗吉尼亚大学、密歇根大学安娜堡分校、北卡罗来纳大学教堂
山分校、英国伦敦政经学院的offer；二是申请国家/地区更具多样性了，如瑞士洛桑酒店管理学院、
法国巴黎政治学院、日本早稻田大学、香港大学；三是申请到一些新的顶尖文理学院和艺术学院，如
罗斯-霍曼理工学院，史密斯学院，汉密尔顿学院，哈弗福德学院，贝茨学院，凯尼恩学院，曼荷莲女
子文理学院，伊斯曼音乐学院，帕森斯设计学院等。
另外，还要特别感谢美国的东北大学、波士顿大学、罗切斯特大学、纽约大学、布兰迪斯、波士顿

content:
奖学金高达两百万美金。
向七德学子抛出橄榄枝的全球顶尖大学有：美国的斯坦福大学，布朗大学，范德堡大学，
埃默里大学，卡内基梅隆大学，弗吉尼亚大学，加州大学伯克利分校，加州大学洛杉矶分校，
南加利福尼亚大学，科尔盖特大学，纽约大学，波士顿大学，还有录取率低至1.9%的密涅瓦大
学。英国的帝国理工大学，圣安德鲁斯大学，杜伦大学，华威大学，伦敦大学学院，巴斯大
学，伯明翰大学，爱丁堡大学，曼彻斯特大学。加拿大的麦吉尔大学，多伦多大学，不列颠哥
伦比亚大学，滑铁卢大学。澳大利亚的墨尔本大学，悉尼大学，新南威尔士大学。亚洲地区有
香港浸会大学。还有不少热爱艺术的同学被世界顶尖的艺术院校录取，如：库伯联盟学院，帕
森斯设计学院，伦敦艺术学院，芝加哥艺术学院，普瑞特艺术学院，加州艺术学院。
祝贺大家！感谢三年来全体师生的共同努力！你们每一个人都是七德当之无愧的骄傲！七
宝德怀特始终秉承为每一位学生的美好人生奠基的教育理念，我们坚信每个学生都是独一
无二的，具有无限潜力与才能。成才之路不是千军万马的独木桥，亦不是平坦宽阔的康庄大
道，每个人需要选择最适合自己的路。有人独爱泛舟湖上的闲情逸致，有人则享受攀登高峰的
惊险刺激，重要的不是结果，而是一路的坚持和心灵的成长。

学入学过程中会面临的困难与挑战。因此，面对未来的不确定性，我们的升学指导团队一直在
与大学保持沟通，将全力帮助大家顺利完成后续的录取工作和入学准备。
祝福我们的2020届毕业生，
感谢全体老师！
让我们期待更多的好消息！

毕业生升学成果
录取概要

春和景明，万象更新。最是一年春好处，鸿雁传书收获时。世外学子经过艰苦卓绝的奋斗，在疫情
后的春天，喜获四方佳讯。2021届学生申请的主流方向依然是美国，同时增加全球布局的多元选
择。在聚焦热门专业、前沿领域的同时，专注于探寻自我的理想和志趣，体现了专业方向的宽广
性、延展性。祝贺世外学子通过三年坚持不懈的努力，不断实现自我成长和自我突破，展现独特卓
越的个性品质。

康奈尔大学、圣母大学等顶尖大学; 威廉姆斯学院、斯沃斯莫尔学院、卡尔顿学院、明德学
院等顶尖文理学院的录取。

S —— Service 学生志愿参加的、无报酬且有学习成长价值的交流活动。

1、活动必须是真实的，活动开始前需制定预期目标，并最终取得明显成果。
2、活动必须经过深思熟虑，并制定详细的计划。
3、活动必须具有可行性，并旨在拓展学生能力。
4、活动必须进行阶段性反思，总结经验克服困难，并通过总结体现个人成长和收获的。
1、在ManageBac上记录所有活动。

4、所有的活动中要注重团队合作活动（CAS project），尝试在不同的project中扮演不同角色，
不能都是个人活动。
5、每个活动都要有照片、每两周进行活动记录、活动总结反思。每学期结束后对本学期每一个

content:
The Arden Shakespeare is now nearly one hundred years old. The
earliest volume in the first series, Edward Dowden's Hamlet, was
published in 1899. Since then the Arden Shakespeare has become
internationally recognized and respected. It is now widely
acknowledged as the pre-eminent Shakespeare series, valued by
scholars, students, actors, and 'the great variety of readers' alike
for its readable and reliable texts, its full annotation and its richly
informative introductions.
We have aimed in the third Arden edition to maintain the
quality and general character of its predecessors, preserving the
commitment to presenting the work as it has been shaped in
history. While each individual volume will necessarily have its
own emphasis in the light of the unique possibilities and
problems posed by the work, the edition as a whole, like the
earlier Ardens, insists upon the highest standards of scholarship
and upon attractive and accessible presentation.
Newly edited from the original quarto and folio editions,
the texts are presented in fully modernized form, with a textual
apparatus that records all substantial divergences from those early
printings. The notes and introductions focus on the conditions
and possibilities of meaning that editors and critics have dis
covered in the work. While building upon the rich history of
scholarly activity that has long shaped our understanding of
Shakespeare's texts, this third series of the Arden Shakespeare is
made necessary and possible by a new generation's encounter with
Shakespeare, engaging with the works and their complex relation
to the culture in which they were - and continue to be - produced.

On each page of the work itself, readers will find a passage of text
supported by commentary and textual notes. In the text itself,
unfamiliar typographic conventions have been avoided in order to
minimize obstacles to the reader. Elided forms in the early texts
are spelt out in full wherever they indicate a usual late-twentieth-
century pronunciation that requires no special indication. Marks
of elision are retained where they are necessary guides to the
scansion and pronunciation of the line. Final -ed in past tense and
participial forms of verbs is always printed as -ed, without accent,
never as -'d, but wherever the required pronunciation diverges
from modern usage a note in the commentary draws attention to
the fact. Where the final -ed should be given syllabic value
contrary to modern usage, e.g.
Lest my bewailed guilt should do thee shame,
(Son 36.10)
the note will take the form
10 bewailed bewailed

Notes in the commentary, for which a major source will be the
Oxford English Dictionary, offer glossarial and other explication of
verbal difficulties; they may also include discussion of points
of interpretation and, in relevant cases, substantial extracts
from Shakespeare's source material. Editors will not usually offer
glossarial notes for words adequately defined in the Concise Oxford
Dictionary or Webster's Ninth New Collegiate Dictionary, but in
cases of doubt they will include notes. Attention, however, will be
drawn to places where more than one likely interpretation can be
proposed and to significant verbal and syntactic complexity. Notes
preceded by  involve discussion of textual variants or readings
emended from the early edition(s) on which the text is based.
x
General Editors' Preface
The textual notes are designed to let readers know when the
edited text diverges from the early edition(s) on which it is
based. Wherever this happens the note will record the rejected
reading of the early edition(s), in original spelling, and the
source of the reading adopted in this edition. Other forms from
the early edition(s) recorded in these notes will include some
spellings of particular interest or significance. The textual notes
take a form that has been in use since the nineteenth century.
This comprises, first: line reference, reading adopted in the
text and closing square bracket; then: abbreviated reference, in
italic, to the earliest edition to adopt the accepted reading, italic
semicolon and noteworthy alternative reading(s), each with
abbreviated italic reference to its source. Distinctive spellings of
the basic text follow the square bracket without indication
of source. Names enclosed in brackets indicate originators of
conjectural emendations when these did not originate in an
edition of the text, or when this edition records a conjecture not
accepted into its text.

Pope's exclamation at the beginning of The Rape of the Lock, 'What
mighty contests rise from trivial things', applies supremely to
Shakespeare s Sonnets. Any and every detail of these poems may be
the occasion of angry dispute, and many have been so, though I
have tried not to get too much involved in such controversies. With
reference to the text of individual sonnets, the minutest features of
spelling, punctuation and format have momentous consequences
for resonance and meaning. I have never felt more strongly than
when working on this text the force of Oscar Wilde's account of a
writer's hard labours: spending the whole morning putting in a
comma, and the whole afternoon taking it out. In the belief not
only that such matters are immensely important, but also that the
1609 Quarto printing reflects the minutiae, as well as the substance,
of a copy manuscript certainly authorized, and perhaps also
penned, by Shakespeare himself, I have attempted to represent the
details of this text as faithfully as the requirements of moderniz
ation will allow. This is, for instance, the first edited text of Sonnets
to include the two pairs of empty parentheses which follow the six-
couplet poem numbered 126. While previous editors have
suggested that these were inserted by the printers, who noticed
that the poem was composed only of twelve lines, not fourteen, I
think this an unlikely intervention. We know that George Eld's
compositors were accustomed to working for such meticulously
niggling writers as Ben Jonson, and a detailed analysis of their
1607-8 publications by Peter Murray suggests that they habitually
reproduced the characteristic spelling forms they encountered,
rather than imposing 'house style'.1
1 Murray, passim.
Xll
Preface
Contextually, also, matters which may not seem immediately of
vital interest or importance here are so. Paramount is the question
of date. The weight of tradition has favoured an early date, placing
Sonnets close in time to the two narrative poems, in 1593-, and
bracketing all three non-dramatic works together as probably
connected with the patronage of the young Henry Wriothesley,
Earl of Southampton. Biographically, for many Victorian and
Edwardian critics, this dating made it possible to sideline Sonnets as
an uncharacteristic, and perhaps in some respects compromising or
even disgraceful, product of Shakespeare's youth. The writing of
them could be seen as a brilliant but embarrassing folly which he
left behind him as his career as a dramatist developed, rather as he
had left behind him his (supposed) early exploits as a poacher of
Sir Thomas Lucy's deer. In the present edition it is proposed that,
on the contrary, though we may never discover how early some
individual sonnets or versions of sonnets were composed, there is
good reason to believe that the whole sequence as published in
1609 was put into its final shape after 1603, and possibly quite close
to its printing. It is for this reason that so much space is given, in
the Introduction, to the issue of dating, for the evidence and
arguments presented here represent a radical departure from
previous study. And as for the compromising or 'disgraceful'
elements of the sonnets: their homoeroticism is here confronted
positively, and is newly contextualized within the powerfully
'homosociaP world of James Fs court. The case for their
association with Southampton largely collapses, but the case for
their connection with William Herbert, Earl of Pembroke,
becomes newly plausible. The 'Pembrokian' hypothesis is re
examined, with the citation of some new supportive evidence. As a
whole, the sequence can be seen, not as a youthful folly, but as the
mature and considered work of a successful professional writer.
Some of what is done here was anticipated in John Kerrigan's
